import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 328

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/328](https://www.erdosproblems.com/328)
- [Er80] Erdős, Paul, *A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory*.
  Ann. Discrete Math. (1980), 89-115.
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial
  number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980).
- [Er80e] Erdős, P., *Some applications of Ramsey's theorem to additive number theory*.
  European J. Combin. (1980), 43-46.
- [NeRo85] J. Nešetřil and V. Rödl, *Two proofs in combinatorial number theory*.
  Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (1985), 185-188.
-/

open AdditiveCombinatorics

namespace Erdos328

/--
Suppose $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ and $C>0$ is such that $1_A\ast 1_A(n)\leq C$ for all
$n\in\mathbb{N}$. Can $A$ be partitioned into $t$ many subsets $A_1,\ldots,A_t$ (where
$t=t(C)$ depends only on $C$) such that $1_{A_i}\ast 1_{A_i}(n)<C$ for all $1\leq i\leq t$
and $n\in \mathbb{N}$?

The answer is no. Asked by Erdős and Newman. Nešetřil and Rödl [NeRo85] have shown the
answer is no for all $C$ (even if $t$ is also allowed to depend on $A$).

Erdős [Er80e] had previously shown the answer is no for $C=3,4$ and infinitely many other
values of $C$.

See also [774].

The linked proof writes the representation function as
`Set.ncard {p : ℕ × ℕ | p.1 ∈ A ∧ p.2 ∈ A ∧ p.1 + p.2 = n}`, which counts the same ordered
pairs as `sumRep`, and states the partition condition as a named definition with the same two
conjuncts used below. Its `∃ t` additionally carries `1 ≤ t`, which costs nothing: `t = 0`
forces `A = ∅`, and `A = {1}` has all representation counts at most `C` for `C ≥ 1`.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Jayyhk/erdos-lean/blob/f8a51976fd2e66a52b4928c109fb9ae877a1a507/problems/328/Erdos328.lean"]
theorem erdos_328 : answer(False) ↔
    ∀ C : ℕ, 0 < C →
      ∃ t : ℕ, ∀ A : Set ℕ, (∀ n, sumRep A n ≤ C) →
        ∃ P : Fin t → Set ℕ, (⋃ i, P i) = A ∧
          Set.univ.PairwiseDisjoint P ∧
          ∀ i, ∀ n, sumRep (P i) n < C := by
  sorry

end Erdos328

findings.description: The historical comments in lines 44–48 incorrectly apply unordered representation-count results to the ordered count used by `sumRep`. In particular, “the answer is no for all C” and “no for C=3,4” are false with the preceding convolution convention: for C=3, two parts always suffice. I proved precisely this partition assertion as `Review328.C3.uniform_three_two` in `/workspace/review/c3.lean`; its axioms are only `propext`, `Classical.choice`, and `Quot.sound`. The actual Lean theorem only negates the global assertion over all C, so it remains faithful to the website's main question; the defect is confined to the historical commentary.
findings.source_evidence: [ErGr80], pp. 48–49, defines f_A using representations n=a_i+a_j with the indices ordered, then states problem 7 and the historical parameter values. https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/80_11_number_theory.pdf . [Er80e], p. 44, explicitly counts three representations when n is the sum of four distinct underlying terms: these are three unordered pairings, but six ordered representations. https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1980-39.pdf . [NeRo85], Theorem 2, concerns B₂^(k) sequences in this unordered convention. The website's LaTeX page repeats the same erroneous transfer to convolution notation, while its definitions page defines convolution as the ordered sum over a+b=n.
findings.suggested_fix: State the historical results explicitly in terms of the papers' unordered representation function or B₂^(k) notation, using a separate parameter k. Remove the claims “no for all C” and “no for C=3” about ordered `sumRep`. The global theorem, its negative answer, and its solved/proof metadata need not change.

reformulations.difference: The linked proof uses a `Set.ncard` representation function, a named partition predicate, and explicitly requires 1 ≤ t. The repository uses `sumRep`, expands the partition conditions, and permits t=0 syntactically.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The representation set equals the finite antidiagonal filtered by membership in A, so its `ncard` equals `sumRep` even when A is infinite. The partition conditions agree after reassociating conjunctions. For every C>0, the singleton {1} satisfies the representation bound. Applying a purported uniform partition size to this singleton produces an element of Fin t, forcing t≥1. I proved the full positive assertions equivalent in `Review328.linked_positive_equivalence`; taking negations gives the required equivalence with the linked theorem.

reformulations.difference: The Lean statement restricts C to positive natural numbers; the source's untyped “C>0” could also be read as permitting positive real bounds.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Integer bounds give exactly the natural-number statement after casting. If a positive real C is not an integer, every integer-valued representation count at most C is already strictly less than C, so the one-part partition works. Thus quantifying over all positive real bounds is equivalent to quantifying over positive natural bounds. This was proved as `Review328.real_bounds_iff_nat_bounds` in `/workspace/review/scratch.lean`.

sources_consulted: https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/Erdos.html — bibliography used to locate the cited papers
https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/ — bibliography used to locate the cited monograph
review.notes: No misformalization of the theorem's formal statement was found relative to the website's literal global question. Its research-solved category and answer(False) match the source. The exact linked proof compiled successfully and its theorem has only the standard three axioms. Boundary checks included empty sets, 0, singletons, ordered off-diagonal pairs, and t=0. The global negative assertion already follows from C=1 and A={1}; this degeneracy is present in the source's stated domain, so it is not reported as a formalization defect. All experiments are under /workspace/review/.
